Costa Rica Imposes Temporary Tariff on Imported Steel Amid Price Volatility

San José—Costa Rica’s Ministry of Economy, Industry and Commerce (MEIC) has imposed a 15% temporary tariff on imported steel bars and rods, a key construction material, in response to what officials describe as “unprecedented price volatility and supply distortions” in the global steel market. The measure, enacted last week and currently in effect, has already begun to reshape the local construction materials industry, prompting both praise and concern from various stakeholders.

According to the official statement released by MEIC, the tariff—applicable to steel bars and rods used primarily in reinforced concrete—will remain in place for an initial period of 180 days. The ministry cited “a surge in low-priced imports from outside the Central American region” as a primary reason for the intervention, arguing that local manufacturers have struggled to compete and that further inaction could jeopardize domestic production capacity.

Industry representatives have welcomed the move. Ana María Jiménez, president of the Costa Rican Construction Materials Association (ACMC), said, “This temporary tariff is a necessary step to prevent unfair competition and preserve thousands of jobs. Domestic producers have faced significant pressure from imports priced well below production costs.” According to ACMC estimates, domestic steel bar producers have seen market share drop by 18% over the past year, a decline attributed largely to increased imports from Asia and Eastern Europe.

However, the new tariff has already led to noticeable changes in the marketplace. Several wholesale distributors in San José and Alajuela report rising prices for finished steel products, with some contractors expressing concern about cost increases for ongoing building projects. “We are seeing immediate price adjustments of 8 to 12% on steel bars, and there is uncertainty about future supply,” said Jorge Salazar, procurement manager at Proconsa, a mid-sized construction materials distributor.

While MEIC maintains that the tariff is designed as a safeguard rather than a long-term protectionist measure, some industry analysts warn that the policy could have mixed outcomes. “The tariff may offer a short-term boost for domestic mills, but it is unclear whether local producers can ramp up output quickly enough to meet demand without driving prices higher,” said Andrés Hidalgo, an independent trade consultant based in San José.

The ministry has pledged to review the effects of the measure within three months, with a decision on any extension to be made based on ongoing market analysis. In the meantime, stakeholders across the construction materials supply chain are bracing for continued volatility as the new tariff regime plays out.
